title: AI keeps stubbornly refusing to take our jobs
gist: Despite near-universal expectation that AI is a job killer, US prime-age employment sits near all-time highs, software developer jobs are rising as a share of the labor force, and firm-level evidence (Census Bureau, Kharazian et al. 2026, The Economist's ~1m AI-created jobs vs ~200k AI-attributed layoffs) shows AI adoption coinciding with more hiring, not less. Smith argues automation's productivity and 'reinstatement' effects are currently matching or exceeding displacement, and that fully agentic AI would be too unreliable to remove humans entirely.

insights.claim: US prime-age employment rate — the best single measure of how many Americans have jobs — continues to hover near all-time highs three-plus years into the generative AI buildout, with no aggregate AI displacement signal.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Aggregate labor data does not support AI-displacement short theses on labor-exposed services; watch prime-age EPOP as the cleanest disconfirming indicator.
insights.quote: The prime-age employment rate — the single best indicator of how many Americans have jobs — continues to hover near all-time highs
insights.locator: So basically, most people think AI is a job-killer

insights.claim: Both Silicon Valley insiders and the general public hold the AI-kills-jobs view largely as an article of faith rather than from concrete argument, with an Ipsos poll showing most Americans expect AI to compete with rather than complement workers and Pew showing that belief strengthening.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A crowded, unexamined consensus on AI job destruction is the setup for repricing if labor data keeps refusing to break.
insights.quote: Most people don’t have concrete arguments for why this should be true; it’s just an article of faith.
insights.locator: I live in San Francisco and hang out

insights.claim: The other macro shocks hitting the current labor market — tariffs and the Iran war — are unambiguously negative for employment, so there is no plausible offsetting positive shock hiding AI-driven job losses other than AI itself.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Removes the 'AI losses are being masked' escape hatch; strengthens the case that displacement simply hasn't shown up yet.
insights.quote: But most of those things — tariffs, the Iran war, etc. — are bad for employment.
insights.locator: Of course, there are lots of other things going on

insights.claim: AI companies spent years marketing their products by predicting humanity's economic obsolescence, and their recent pivot to 'AI will create jobs' messaging is plausibly an honest update rather than a cynical PR move to defuse public outrage.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Read AI-lab messaging shifts as genuine timeline revisions, which matters for how fast enterprise AI revenue from labor substitution can actually ramp.
insights.quote: This is why the AI companies’ recent messaging pivot — many now say that AI will create jobs rather than destroying them — may be honest, rather than a cynical marketing ploy to calm public outrage.
insights.locator: This is why the AI companies’ recent messaging pivot

insights.claim: Acemoglu and Restrepo's three-channel framework — displacement, productivity, and reinstatement (new tasks where labor has comparative advantage) — is the right lens for AI, and AI doomers typically model only the first channel.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Use the three-channel framework to underwrite labor-exposed businesses: net headcount effect depends on reinstatement, not substitution rates.
insights.quote: The reinstatement effect is the polar opposite of the displacement effect and directly increases the labor share as well as labor demand.
insights.locator: Here are Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019)

insights.claim: Productivity gains also create jobs through product variety, an under-modeled channel: as carmakers got more productive they produced more makes, models and colors, and GM overtook Ford by offering more variety rather than more units.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Expect AI productivity gains to show up as proliferation of SKUs, features and content variety — a demand-expanding, headcount-supportive outcome.
insights.quote: GM famously overtook Ford by offering more models, more frequent model updates, and more colors.
insights.locator: footnote: Higher task-level productivity can destroy jobs

insights.claim: Replacing tasks is categorically different from replacing jobs, because modern jobs are pieces of a complex value-producing machine whose mechanism individual workers often cannot see.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Task-exposure scores (the basis of most AI-displacement research and screens) systematically overstate job risk; discount them when sizing labor-disruption trades.
insights.quote: Modern jobs are much more than a simple collection of tasks — they are pieces of a complex machine that produces value in ways that an individual worker often doesn’t even see.
insights.locator: It seems like we’re uncovering a consistent human blind spot

insights.claim: Daron Acemoglu's skepticism rests on the assumption that AI-created new tasks will be 'bad tasks' like misinformation and cybercrime, an assumption the current firm-level evidence does not support.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The leading academic bear case on AI and labor rests on an assumption now contradicted by data — a reason to fade AI-pessimist policy narratives.
insights.quote: AI detractors, meanwhile — like Daron Acemoglu himself — often simply assume that new tasks created by AI will be “bad tasks”
insights.locator: Anecdotally, a lot of tech people think

themes.theme: Firm-level evidence: adoption correlates with hiring

insights.claim: In the Census Bureau's AI survey running since 2023, most firms report no employment change from AI, but among firms reporting a change, more reported an employment increase than a decrease.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Firm-level survey evidence cuts against the mass-layoff narrative; a reason to stay long labor-intensive services rather than short them on AI.
insights.quote: Most companies reported no change in overall employment, which could just be due to inertia. But of companies that did report a change, more reported an increase than a decrease!
insights.locator: Alex Tabarrok recently reported on a Census Bureau survey

insights.claim: Among firms using AI, 44% say it supplemented or enhanced work an employee already does, only 10% say it performed a task an employee used to do, and 11% say it introduced a task nobody had been doing.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Net task creation (11%) is roughly equal to net task destruction (10%) — quantify AI's labor effect with these ratios rather than vendor claims.
insights.quote: Among firms using AI, 44% say it supplemented or enhanced work an employee already does. Ten percent say it performed a task an employee used to do. Eleven percent say it introduced a task no one had been doing.
insights.locator: The story was similar for tasks. Tabarrok writes

insights.claim: Kharazian, Simon, and Stevens (2026), using company-level data, find that firms adopting more AI tend to hire humans rather than replace them — and the same holds for entry-level jobs widely assumed to be most at risk.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Entry-level hiring collapse is a popular AI-disruption narrative; the best available company-level dataset contradicts it — watch for revisions before positioning on it.
insights.locator: Rigorous research, meanwhile, sometimes finds negative effects

insights.claim: Software developer employment as a share of the US labor force is near its all-time high and on a steep uptrend even in the era of Codex and Claude Code, and firms that replaced engineers with AI have had to rehire many of them, sometimes at a premium.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The single most AI-exposed white-collar occupation is expanding, not shrinking — a direct check on 'AI kills SaaS headcount' theses and dev-tools demand assumptions.
insights.quote: organizations that thought they could replace lots of their software engineers with AI ended up having to hire many of them back — sometimes at a premium.
insights.locator: This helps explain why in the age of Codex and Claude Code

themes.theme: Data-center buildout as the visible labor demand channel

insights.claim: The Economist estimates AI has created roughly 1 million new US jobs so far, dwarfing the roughly 200,000 layoffs attributed to AI since mid-2023 and more than offsetting weaker back-office hiring.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A 5:1 created-to-destroyed ratio is the headline number to cite against AI-unemployment narratives; monitor whether the layoff side starts compounding.
insights.quote: The Economist estimates that AI has so far created around 1m new jobs in America. That easily exceeds the roughly 200,000 lay-offs attributed to AI since mid-2023
insights.locator: The Economist, meanwhile, has a report

insights.claim: Across five industries at the heart of the data-center build-out — from electrical contracting to equipment manufacturing — employment has risen roughly 320,000 above trend since 2023, and LinkedIn counts nearly half a million data-center jobs created in America between 2023 and 2025.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Confirms the electrical/industrial supply chain as the real-economy transmission of AI capex — relevant to electrical equipment and contracting exposure.
insights.quote: The Economist tracked five industries at the heart of the data-centre build-out, from electrical contracting to equipment manufacturing. Since 2023 employment in them has risen by roughly 320,000 more than broader…trends would suggest
insights.locator: America’s AI infrastructure splurge

insights.claim: Wage inflation is concentrated in the AI physical build-out: data-center installation and maintenance jobs advertise about 40% higher pay than comparable work elsewhere, and in the year to June average hourly earnings rose over 13% in electrical-equipment manufacturing and nearly 8% among electrical contractors.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Skilled-trades wage inflation is a real and rising cost input to data-center capex budgets, and a margin risk for contractors bidding fixed-price work.
insights.quote: In the year to June, average hourly earnings rose more than 13% in electrical-equipment manufacturing and nearly 8% among electrical contractors.
insights.locator: The scramble for workers is showing up in pay cheques

insights.claim: A new white-collar job class is forming around AI — model engineers, data annotators, 'forward-deployed' engineers, and 'heads of AI' — with LinkedIn postings for heads of AI, AI engineers and directors of AI roughly doubling since 2023-24.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Job-posting growth in these titles is a cleaner real-time proxy for enterprise AI adoption depth than vendor-reported ARR.
insights.quote: Postings for heads of AI, AI engineers and directors of AI have roughly doubled since 2023-24, according to LinkedIn
insights.locator: AI is also creating a new class of white-collar jobs

insights.claim: Gad Levanon of the Burning Glass Institute estimates roughly 1% of professional jobs are now 'AI jobs', while professional occupations closest to the AI boom — engineers, software developers, mathematicians and data scientists — have added roughly 730,000 jobs above trend.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sizes the AI-native labor pool: still ~1% of professional employment, implying a long runway of AI-driven hiring rather than a completed shift.
insights.quote: reckons roughly 1% of professional jobs are now “AI jobs”
insights.locator: Preliminary research by Gad Levanon

insights.claim: Modern occupations are far harder to eliminate than historical ones because they are 'messy' bundles of many different tasks — unlike elevator operators or manual typesetters, travel agents survived the internet in reduced but substantial numbers.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Occupational-obsolescence bets should target narrow single-task roles, not messy multi-task professions; the latter shrink slowly if at all.
insights.quote: travel agents do a whole lot of different tasks, so they’re harder to replace than people who just stand there and press a button.
insights.locator: The reason is probably that the job of “travel agent”

insights.claim: Human translator employment in the US is more or less stable and projected to stay stable over the next decade, despite translation appearing to be the most obviously automatable white-collar task — because there is effectively no ceiling on how much content can be translated.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The clearest natural experiment in AI substitution produced no net job loss — strong evidence that demand elasticity absorbs capability gains.
insights.quote: If you could go back to 2022, and tell people that in four years, AI would be solving frontier math problems, but we’d still have the same number of people working as translators, how many would have believed you?
insights.locator: The most impressive example might be translators

insights.claim: Top AI researchers who predicted the end of human radiologists were confounded, with Geoffrey Hinton now publicly explaining why he was wrong, and truckers are also doing fine.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The two canonical AI-displacement predictions both failed — a base rate to apply to current confident forecasts of occupational extinction.
insights.locator: Top AI researchers who famously predicted the end of human radiologists

themes.theme: The fear-vs-reality gap and the agentic-AI bottleneck

insights.claim: Hartley et al. (2026) find fear of AI job replacement is extremely common and rises with a worker's AI exposure — the more of the day people spend using AI at work, the more afraid they are — yet the authors found zero correlation between AI exposure and actual job loss.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Worker sentiment is a broken signal for labor displacement; do not use survey-based AI anxiety as a leading indicator for employment cuts.
insights.quote: the more of their day people spend using AI at work, the more they’re afraid of being replaced
insights.locator: Hartley et al. (2026) have a really excellent paper

insights.claim: Workers systematically overestimate their own replaceability because they do not actually know how they produce value at their jobs — which also explains why high-paying jobs can feel like 'bullshit' to those doing them.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A structural bias that will keep generating false AI-displacement scares; useful for fading sentiment-driven selloffs in labor-heavy sectors.
insights.quote: People don’t actually know how they produce value at their jobs.
insights.locator: It seems like we’re uncovering a consistent human blind spot

insights.claim: Sam Altman has publicly admitted he was wrong on AI's timeline, expecting much more disruption and software businesses 'up for grabs' quickly after GPT-4 in 2023, and now says society and the economy will adapt more slowly.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The most aggressive AI-disruption forecaster has extended his own timeline — reduces urgency of 'SaaS is dead' repricing.
insights.quote: I thought when we got to GPT-4, which was back in 2023, that very quickly after that there was going to be much more disruption, software businesses up for grabs right away,
insights.locator: AI leaders are starting to realize

insights.claim: Wholesale human job replacement requires AI to become far more agentic, and greater agency inherently makes AI less reliable from a human point of view — so humans will always have jobs keeping AI agents on track.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If reliability scales inversely with agency, the addressable market is AI supervision tooling and human-in-the-loop services, not headcount elimination.
insights.quote: So I predict that humans will always have jobs keeping AI agents on track.
insights.locator: But my bet is that while many occupations

insights.claim: Even granting that an AI job apocalypse eventually arrives, it is not coming soon and is definitively not present now — the displacement trade is a long-dated option, not a current-year thesis.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Timing matters more than direction: positioning for AI-driven labor collapse carries multi-year carry costs with no visible catalyst.
insights.quote: it doesn’t seem like it’s coming soon, and it certainly isn’t here right now
insights.locator: Even if I’m wrong, though
